Menu.name: Menu
Menu.doc:
The record-driven menu (planes.md §4–§6): items are DATA — the component
arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS
menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }

- `key` renders right-aligned (display only — registration is the Keys
  service's, later).
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.

  This was THREE mechanisms before the icon set landed: a text glyph (`"◐"`), a
  hardcoded `"lightbulb"` that special-cased its way to a drawn bulb because no
  glyph matched, and `iconKind` naming a class. The middle one was the tell —
  somebody needed a mark the fonts could not give, and the escape hatch already
  existed. One field now; a COMPUTED name needs its class kept with
  `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow; the cascade itself
  lands with the roving-keyboard stage).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's CONTENT with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.

Declared ONCE, opened by many (the worked example): rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
RAISE the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app.

Dismissal: the BACKDROP (a full-app child under the panel) — a press
outside closes AND is swallowed, the Mac rule (planes.md §12.1, resolved
for v1); Escape closes; pick closes after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

MenuBar.menus.name: menus
MenuBar.menus.doc:
The whole bar as **data**: `[ { id, label, bold?, kind?, items: [ …menu records… ] } ]`,
where `items` is exactly `Menu`'s record shape. **One internal `Menu` serves every
title**, deriving its rows from the open one — so item state stays live while a menu is
up, and there is nothing to keep in step. Because the records are the single
declaration, an app can derive its keyboard-shortcut registry from the same array the
bar renders.

MenuBar.name: MenuBar
MenuBar.doc:
The record-driven menu bar (planes.md §4–§6): whole menus are DATA —

    menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] }

— and the component arranges. ONE internal Menu serves every title; its
`items` constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state
(enabled, checked, labels) stays LIVE while the menu is up. Because the
records are the single declaration, an app can derive its key registry
from the same array the bar renders — nothing is declared twice (the
Newton keys direction, proven in apps/desktop).

Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do NOT highlight on mere hover;
a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving
across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes.

Delivery is the one seam: `picked(id)` — override at the use site.

```declare
App [ width = 380, height = 120, chose: string = "",
    bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8,
        menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }),
                                                          ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }),
                    ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }),
                                                           ({ divider: true }),
                                                           ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

Dialog.name: Dialog
Dialog.doc:
The modal tier (planes.md): a full-app SCRIM that swallows every press —
modal input blocking, no light dismiss — under a centered panel with a
focusTrap. Buttons are RECORDS (the records door): `{ id, label,
default?, cancel? }`, rendered as themed library Buttons right-aligned in
the platform arrangement. Focus SAVES on open and RETURNS on close.

Keyboard: Return picks the DEFAULT button (the Cupertino rule; a focused
button also activates on Space/Enter — the pick guard makes the double
harmless), Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just
closes.

The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id
(the `picked(id)` override remains the declarative seam):

    dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.")
    dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …)
    dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.")

`ask` is Cancel / No / Yes-default; `error` renders the title in the
theme's errorColor.

Platform STRUCTURE is data (the scheme): `dialogWidth`,
`dialogButtons` = "end" (a right-aligned row — SF, Material) | "stack"
(the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, DEFAULT ON TOP) | "fill"
(WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row),
`dialogAlign` = "left" | "center" (the Cupertino centered title),
`dialogTitleSize` / `dialogBodySize`. Plus scrimColor + scrimOpacity
(Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by SHADOW; Material's spec scrim is
32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, errorColor.

**Declare one and call it.** A `Dialog` is not a view you show and hide around your
content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves
every prompt in the program.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 140, said: string = "",
    dlg: Dialog [ ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…",
        onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.",
                                (id) => { app.said = id }) }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ]
    ]
```

Keyboard: Return picks the DEFAULT button (the Cupertino rule; a focused

theme's errorColor.

Platform STRUCTURE is data (the scheme): `dialogWidth`,
`dialogButtons` = "end" (a right-aligned row — SF, Material) | "stack"
(the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, DEFAULT ON TOP) | "fill"
(WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row),
`dialogAlign` = "left" | "center" (the Cupertino centered title),
`dialogTitleSize` / `dialogBodySize`. Plus scrimColor + scrimOpacity
(Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by SHADOW; Material's spec scrim is
32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, errorColor.

**Declare one and call it.** A `Dialog` is not a view you show and hide around your
content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves
every prompt in the program.

AppIsland.program.name: program
AppIsland.program.doc:
What to run: a program name, a relative path (`"../../calendar/calendar"` reaches the
real app — **no copy of the source, ever**), or the reserved `"__raw__"` live-edit
channel, where the running program is the host app's `liveSource` and recompiles as it
changes. **`""` detaches the island** and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel
stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a
view of itself.

AppIsland.env.name: env
AppIsland.env.doc:

child's reactive `app.env` at mount **and on every change**. Empty sends none, so the
child keeps its own defaults — leave it alone unless the host genuinely overrides
something, or you will pin the child's appearance against the system's.

AppIsland.name: AppIsland
AppIsland.doc:
`AppIsland` embeds a live Declare application: give it a `program` and it mounts
that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and
stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills
the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view.

It composes `DOMIsland` (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the
host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the
`run:…` wire. The page host (`browser/host-client.js`) sees the key on the box,
resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile,
identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child.

`childName` (inherited from `DOMIsland`) is the reverse channel: the running child's
`appName` reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

SimpleLayout.method.place.name: place
SimpleLayout.method.place.doc:

**The cross axis and every size stay the children's own** — a child centres itself
across a row with the ordinary `y = center`. Override it in a subclass for custom
geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the one place

SimpleLayout.name: SimpleLayout
SimpleLayout.doc:
The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

WrappingLayout.method.place.doc:
Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. **It owns
both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than

WrappingLayout.name: WrappingLayout
WrappingLayout.doc:
A horizontal flow that WRAPS: children run left to right
`spacing` apart, and when the next one would overflow the view's width it
drops to a new row (`lineSpacing` down; -1, the default, means "same as
spacing"). With room for one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it
stacks — cards that reflow on a phone with no media query. It owns BOTH
axes of each child (a flow is 2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `align`
justifies each finished row: `start` (left, the default) or `center` (a row
that does not fill the width sits centered).

Division of labor: this is the tool for UNIFORM, replicated collections
that reflow by fitting. Managing NAMED regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
    ]
```

ResponsiveLayout.plan.name: plan
ResponsiveLayout.plan.doc:
The storyboard: a list of `{ from, flow, share?, gap? }` entries. **`from` means "use
this plan when the view is at least this wide"** — the largest `from` that fits wins,
wherever it sits in the list, and `from: 0` is the fallback. `flow` is `"row"` or
`"stack"`. `share` divides the width among the children it **names by their own child
names**, checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error.
**A share of `0` hides that child while the plan is active**, so "the actions disappear
on small screens" is one number, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A
child a plan does not name keeps its natural width.

ResponsiveLayout.method.place.name: place
ResponsiveLayout.method.place.doc:

arranges accordingly. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much
room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A
plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business.

ResponsiveLayout.name: ResponsiveLayout
ResponsiveLayout.doc:
A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. `share` divides the width (what is left of it
after the gaps) among the children it NAMES — the names are the view's own
child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is
a loud error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **`0` hides that child while
the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a
number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view
widens. A child a plan does NOT name is left alone: natural width, the flow
just places it. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry
its own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children
keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as
always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On
the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary
literals (`y = center` in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack
at all — *shares fill; naturals align.*

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages NAMED regions. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State` applied on a
width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding `place()` —
the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

Spacer.flexes.name: flexes
Spacer.flexes.doc:
The marker a flow layout looks for. True (the default) means the layout owns this
Spacer's size along the flow axis and expands it to take up the slack — which is
what makes `Spacer [ ]` push its siblings apart. Set it false for a fixed gap you
size yourself.

Spacer.name: Spacer
Spacer.doc:
When a row (or stack)
does not fill its container, the leftover space has to go SOMEWHERE — and
the laid children cannot take it themselves (their flow-axis slot is owned
by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two
groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each
side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns.
Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan
whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply
zero and invisible in effect.

The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so
a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the
`flexes` marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise —
it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

Table.method.deleteRequested.name: deleteRequested
Table.method.deleteRequested.doc:
**Delivery seam — the app declares what deleting is.** Fires on Delete or Backspace
while there is a selection *and the table itself holds focus*, so a text field's
Backspace is never mistaken for it. Does nothing by default: refusal by inertness.

Table.name: Table
Table.doc:
The list collection, componentized (docs/system-design/component-briefs.md §2 —
D8 RULED): the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or
written) collection, carrying the RULED selection model
(docs/system-design/selection-model.md) so no app hand-rolls it again:

- **Selection is the Table's VALUE** — `selected` (the primary member) and
  `selection` (all of them, presented order), holding MEMBERS: the record for
  a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via
  `input` (Contract 1 form b); identity per the ruled ladder (a record's `id`
  by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule).
- **The three facts**: selection, the ANCHOR (where ranges extend from), and
  the keyboard position `active` — moved by arrows, extended by shift,
  walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection).
- **`selects` declares the mode**: `none | single | multi` (default single).
  (Build note: the ruled docs used one word for the mode AND the value; the
  value keeps the ruled name `selection`, so the mode rides `selects`.)
- Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children
  reaching their table as `parent`, replicated over data or written by hand.
  The row template stays free of any selection wiring.
- Windowing composes: put `virtualize` on the row template and selection,
  ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the DATA
  through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row
  can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (uniform
  row extents, the kernel's own v1 assumption).

    Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel },
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30,
            t: Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ] ] ]

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 200,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" },
                             { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" },
                             { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } },
    t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26,
            Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ]
            ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ]
    ]
```

TableRow.selected.name: selected
TableRow.selected.doc:
On a **`Table`**, the primary selected *member* — the record most recently selected, or
`null`. On a **`TableRow`**, whether this row's member is in that selection, derived
from the table and never stored. Both are members-not-views: **selection survives sorts,
filters, and windowing** because it was never a set of instances.

whether this row is that one.

Combobox.name: Combobox
Combobox.doc:
Filter-as-you-type over a collection (component-briefs.md §3 — D8 RULED): a
text field owning a QUERY plus a dismissable option list owning a CHOICE — the
canonical derived selection over data. Composition, not invention: TextInput
for the entry, the Menu machinery for the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss,
Escape closes — the whole dismissal discipline rides along), and the matches
are a DERIVED collection — a constraint over the items array, so the live
match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned.

    Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ]

- **Items are members** (the selection model's currency): records — shown by
  their `label` (or `id`) — or plain strings. `value` holds the CHOSEN member;
  `input(v)` is the delivery seam (Contract 1): the default writes `value`, a
  use-site override redirects and the slot stays untouched.
- **Typing filters live** (case-insensitive substring); opening WITHOUT typing
  shows the full list (the disclosure-button read). Picking echoes the label
  into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text.
- **Keyboard**: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved
  row — or the FIRST match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path);
  Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the
  focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own.
- The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and
  `virtualize` applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes).

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "",
    people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] },
    Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people },
        input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ]
    ]
```

ContextMenu.method.open.name: open
ContextMenu.method.open.doc:
Opens the menu **anchored at the pointer**, given the serving view and the pointer
event — `Menu.openAt` under the name the two-line wiring reads best with. **The serving
view declares the gesture, and that declaration is what routes it**: `onContextMenu`
engages the right-click and two-finger path, `onHold` the touch long-press. Neither
engages anywhere a handler is not declared, so a context menu costs nothing on views
that do not offer one.

ContextMenu.name: ContextMenu
ContextMenu.doc:
The right-click / long-press menu (component-briefs.md §4 — D8 RULED): Menu's
machinery WHOLE — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport
clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (outside press closes AND is swallowed),
Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. No new overlay
machinery, by the brief's own constraint: if ContextMenu ever needs something
Menu lacks, Menu grows it and both ride.

Declared ONCE, opened by many. The SERVING view declares the gesture — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.


docSegs.md:
The right-click / long-press menu (component-briefs.md §4 — D8 RULED): Menu's
machinery WHOLE — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport
clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (outside press closes AND is swallowed),
Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. No new overlay
machinery, by the brief's own constraint: if ContextMenu ever needs something
Menu lacks, Menu grows it and both ride.

Declared ONCE, opened by many. The SERVING view declares the gesture — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.

DataGrid.name: DataGrid
DataGrid.doc:
The Table contract plus a COLUMN MODEL (component-briefs.md §5 — D8 RULED):
headers, sortable, reorderable and resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a
windowed collection — the header drags are the forcing case the axis-scoped
`claim = x` was designed for.

    DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 70 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ]

- **Columns are written members** (`Column` — selection-model §1b: permanent,
  authored, identity = the child): `title` heads the column, `field` names
  what a cell shows, `width` is the authored width — a PLAIN value (the
  column model derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive
  width belongs in the grid's `widths` state, which IS a tracked dep:
  `widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }`). A column's id is its
  `field` (title as fallback).
- **Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state** (Contract 1 form b):
  `order` (column ids, presented order) and `widths` (id → width overrides).
  Reorder delivers through `arrangeInput(order)`, resize through
  `resizeInput(id, w)` — defaults write the slots; an app override owns them
  (persisted layouts). Widths are PLAIN VALUES — nothing measures cells.
- **Header interactions**: click sorts — a DELIVERY (`sortInput(on, dir)`
  writing `sortOn`/`sortDir` by default): sort NAMES a derivation, the truth
  stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the
  order its collection has). Horizontal drag REORDERS (live swap at the
  midpoint); the right-edge grip RESIZES. Both drags declare `claim = x` —
  on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x.
- **Rows**: the use site writes ONE bare `GridRow` template over its rows
  path — cells generate from the column model, each showing `record[field]`.
  Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — `virtualize` on the
  template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets
  the window's geometry (the kernel's leading anchor).
- Focus: land-as-one-stop, browse mode (arrows navigate rows). Entry-mode
  grids (`focusScope = capture`, the tax-form convention) are a later
  increment; nothing here forecloses it.
- AT: rows speak logical position (the Surface seam). The column dimension
  (`aria-colcount`/`colindex`) is DEFERRED to the same seam — noted, not
  wired, in v1.
- Narrow widths: v1 clips (`clip` on the cell); the deliberate degrade
  (priority, not squish) is a designed later increment per the brief.

Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are `Table`'s, documented there. What follows
is only the column model.

```declare
App [ width = 440, height = 220,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail",      "state": "open" },
                             { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" },
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 50 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]
        ]
    ]
```

click a header to sort.

GridRow.name: GridRow
GridRow.doc:
The Table contract plus a COLUMN MODEL (component-briefs.md §5 — D8 RULED):
headers, sortable, reorderable and resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a
windowed collection — the header drags are the forcing case the axis-scoped
`claim = x` was designed for.

    DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 70 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ]

- **Columns are written members** (`Column` — selection-model §1b: permanent,
  authored, identity = the child): `title` heads the column, `field` names
  what a cell shows, `width` is the authored width — a PLAIN value (the
  column model derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive
  width belongs in the grid's `widths` state, which IS a tracked dep:
  `widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }`). A column's id is its
  `field` (title as fallback).
- **Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state** (Contract 1 form b):
  `order` (column ids, presented order) and `widths` (id → width overrides).
  Reorder delivers through `arrangeInput(order)`, resize through
  `resizeInput(id, w)` — defaults write the slots; an app override owns them
  (persisted layouts). Widths are PLAIN VALUES — nothing measures cells.
- **Header interactions**: click sorts — a DELIVERY (`sortInput(on, dir)`
  writing `sortOn`/`sortDir` by default): sort NAMES a derivation, the truth
  stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the
  order its collection has). Horizontal drag REORDERS (live swap at the
  midpoint); the right-edge grip RESIZES. Both drags declare `claim = x` —
  on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x.
- **Rows**: the use site writes ONE bare `GridRow` template over its rows
  path — cells generate from the column model, each showing `record[field]`.
  Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — `virtualize` on the
  template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets
  the window's geometry (the kernel's leading anchor).
- Focus: land-as-one-stop, browse mode (arrows navigate rows). Entry-mode
  grids (`focusScope = capture`, the tax-form convention) are a later
  increment; nothing here forecloses it.
- AT: rows speak logical position (the Surface seam). The column dimension
  (`aria-colcount`/`colindex`) is DEFERRED to the same seam — noted, not
  wired, in v1.
- Narrow widths: v1 clips (`clip` on the cell); the deliberate degrade
  (priority, not squish) is a designed later increment per the brief.

```declare
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 50 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]
        ]
    ]
```

Segmented.name: Segmented
Segmented.doc:
A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options
are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are **data**, like
`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

```declare-fragment
Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page },
    choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }),
                 ({ id: "table",    label: "Table" }),
                 ({ id: "grid",     label: "DataGrid" }) ] },
    input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
    ]
```

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

It is also the mainstream shape. Most native toolkits take segments as titles in an array,
picks from a `ForEach`, Ant Design takes `options`; only Material and WinUI name
the item at all, and both compound it. A bare `Segment` class was the minority
pattern — and bare enough that two apps in this corpus had taken the name for a
paragraph of prose.

### Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a DESIGN decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view
tree, not the layout strategy whose job that is. Three reasons not to:

- **The systems that call this a segmented control agree.** The native ones
  divide evenly by default, as does the classic
  segmented `Picker`. The ones that size to content — Bootstrap, Ant — are really
  styling a row of buttons.
- **The segmented convention makes it a content rule**: keep segment labels short and
  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.
- **The sliding pill.** At equal widths it translates at constant width. At
  variable widths it would have to morph its width WHILE travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly: **a `Segmented` does not self-size to
its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

### The pill

The highlight springs a NORMALIZED LANE — a float index — not pixels. `x` is then
`lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes `segW` and the pill **snaps** to the right
place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. Calendar's tab
strip discovered this; it is the one thing the bespoke copies did better than the
library, and it is now here.

The look is the library's: the chosen segment wears a raised `surface` pill with
a hairline. The motion is calendar's. Neither app was wrong about the half it got
right (`chrome-divergences.md` D9).

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one",
    Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page },
        choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }),
                     ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }),
                     ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] },
        input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ]
    ]
```

MoonIcon.name: MoonIcon
MoonIcon.doc:
"Dark" in the appearance triad. The crescent is **the region between two equal
circles**, the second offset by (3, −3) — so both arcs meet exactly at the circles'
intersection points and the horns close to a point instead of leaving the ragged tail
an arc pair leaves.

Renders the half-filled disc.

AutoIcon.name: AutoIcon
AutoIcon.doc:
"System" in the appearance triad — the same disc, half of it taken away. **The ring
stays around the empty half** so it reads as part of one object rather than as a gap.
The one mark of the three whose meaning *is* its fill, which is why a mixed
outline-and-filled language is right for the triad.

Icon.ink.name: ink
Icon.ink.doc:
The mark's colour. Follows the **prevailing `textColor`**, so an icon beside a muted
label goes muted on its own. **The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide**,
so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a
dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets one — `IconHost` does it for
every icon built by name.

Icon.weight.name: weight
Icon.weight.doc:
Stroke width in **final device pixels, not authored ones**. Divide by `unit` inside
`draw` (`d.lineWidth = weight / unit`) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a
constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among.

Icon.unit.name: unit
Icon.unit.doc:
The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. **Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by
it.** Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants.

Icon.name: Icon
Icon.doc:
A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. Fonts are not UI objects:
their glyphs are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The house
already knew this in three places before it had a name for it (`Checkbox.mark`,
`Menu.check`, `Combobox.disc` are all drawn); this is that decision, stated once.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is ONE path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px, which is every site in this corpus, that is
invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a
mark — so **this set is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an
empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth =
weight` *outside* the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon
systems take a third road and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger
undertaking than this set needs.

`test/probe/iconbook.declare` shows the ramp — the same chevron and bulb at 16,
24, 32, 48 and 64 — if the tradeoff ever needs re-judging.

### What is NOT an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution
(`dom-backend.ts` `rasterize()`), while `scale` is a CSS transform applied
*after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them.
Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling
inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records AND reallocates the backing
canvas every frame, which is what dragged the dock's magnification from 60 to
~25fps (`adaptive-draw-cache.md`). A static size re-records once and costs
nothing after. Measured: 120 icons re-recording their *content* every frame runs
frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the prevailing text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

IconHost.kind.name: kind
IconHost.kind.doc:
The icon **class name** to build (`"TrashIcon"`). `""` builds nothing and the host
collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. **Consumed once,
at construction** — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name
that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

IconHost.ink.name: ink
IconHost.ink.doc:
The colour handed to the icon this host builds. **`createView` cannot pass attributes,
so a prevailing slot is the only channel that reaches it** — this publishes `textColor`
for exactly that. Defaults to `theme.text` rather than the platform's inherited black,
which is what stops a host-built icon from rendering invisibly on a dark surface.

IconHost.event.init.name: init
IconHost.event.init.doc: Builds the named icon. Fires once.

docSegs.md: Builds the named icon. Fires once.

IconHost.name: IconHost
IconHost.doc:
A control names its icon (`iconLeft = TrashIcon`) rather than nesting one,
   because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and
   because an attribute is the one form where AUTHORED and BOUND are the same
   mechanism. `IconHost` is what turns that name into a live view, through the
   same `app.createView` seam the menu's `iconKind` already uses.

   It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only
   the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special
   case.

   LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction.
   A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not
   served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes
   on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this
   corpus names its icon statically.

SegmentedItem.ink.name: ink
SegmentedItem.ink.doc:
This segment's text and icon colour, brightening when it is on or hot. One slot, so a

SegmentedItem.location.name: location
SegmentedItem.location.doc:
Makes this segment a **real link**: give a choice a `location` and the segment navigates
there in its own `onClick`. This is what keeps a view-switching control visible to link
extraction — the crawler reads `app.location = …` out of activation handlers, and
`input(v)` is not one, since its destination depends on a value that does not exist at
extraction time. Empty for an ordinary segmented control, and an empty read emits no
anchor.

SegmentedItem.name: SegmentedItem
SegmentedItem.doc:
One choice of a `Segmented`, **materialized from that control's `choices` data — never
authored directly**, which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full
`Control`: its own tab stop, activated by Space or Enter, so a user can tab to an
inactive choice and select it.

It renders rest, hover and press only. **The chosen state is the sliding pill behind
these, not a fill of its own** — which is exactly what lets the pill travel between
segments instead of popping.

ArrowIcon.name: ArrowIcon
ArrowIcon.doc:
An arrow, **not a chevron** — the two mean different things and must not look alike.
A chevron *discloses*; an arrow points at a direction that **is itself the state**:
sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. Tracker had
the two adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape
for both read as a mistake.

tree.name: View
tree.doc:
The base of every visual thing in Declare — a rectangular **box** with a position, a
size, and decoration (fill, corner radius, border, shadow). Everything you see
descends from `View`: `Text`, `Image`, your own `class … extends View`. A plain
`View` is a colored box; give it children and it becomes a container.

Its geometry is set two ways that read the same: literal (`width = 200`) or a reactive
`{ }` constraint the runtime keeps true (`width = { parent.width }`). Children nest
inside the brackets, so the source shape mirrors the visual shape; *how* they are
arranged is the `layout` attribute, not the container's type.

```declare
View [ width = 200, height = 120, fill = white, cornerRadius = 8,
    Text [ text = "hello", x = 12, y = 12 ]
    ]
```

Every attribute below can be asked about in a **running** program:
`window.__declare.explain(path, attr)` returns the live value *and* its provenance
(the owning constraint, its source, its reads); `__declare.help()` lists the calls.
See `docs/operational/introspection.md`.

attributes.name: x
attributes.doc:
The horizontal offset within the parent, in pixels. Honoured only while the parent
imposes no `layout` — **a layout overwrites `x` every pass**, so use it for absolute
placement (the layout-none default) and switch to `layout` for arrangement; don't fight
one with the other.

imposes no `layout` — **a layout overwrites `x` every pass**, so use it for absolute
placement (the layout-none default) and switch to `layout` for arrangement; don't fight
one with the other.

attributes.name: y
attributes.doc:
The vertical offset within the parent — the twin of `x`, and likewise overwritten by a
parent `layout`.

docSegs.md:
The vertical offset within the parent — the twin of `x`, and likewise overwritten by a
parent `layout`.

attributes.name: width
attributes.doc:
The box's width, in **pixels** (`Length`). Defaults to `0`, so a container with no
width set collapses — give it one, a `{ }` constraint, or `100%` (parent-relative).
Set it live and children constrained to it reflow in the same frame; there is no
re-layout call. To size *to* content instead, constrain it: `width = { Math.min(contentWidth, 480) }`.

attributes.name: height
attributes.doc:
The box's height in pixels (`Length`), mirroring `width`. `0` by default. A `Text`
left unsized takes its natural measured height, so you usually set `height` only to
clip or to drive a layout.

attributes.name: fill
attributes.doc:
What paints the box: a solid `Color` or a `gradient(…)` — the one slot, subsuming a
plain background color. `null` (the default) paints **nothing** — an unfilled box is
invisible but still lays out and still catches clicks. In a `[ ]` literal a color is
`#RRGGBB`; inside a `{ }` body it is `0xRRGGBB` (the one place the spelling differs).

```declare
View [ fill = { gradient("90deg", 0x1E2A36, 0x0B141B) } ]
```

attributes.name: cornerRadius
attributes.doc:
Rounds the **painted** box by this many pixels (default `0`, square). It shapes fill,
border, and shadow — but not hit-testing or clipping: the box stays a rectangle for
layout and clicks. To clip children to the rounded shape, set `clip = true` as well.

attributes.name: hovered
attributes.doc:
True while the pointer is over this view — read-only, maintained by the same hit walk that
routes presses, so it agrees with what a click would reach. Read it in a constraint rather
than tracking enter/leave by hand: `fill = { hovered ? theme.control : null }`. On a touch
device there is no hovering, so gate mouse-only affordances on `app.touchDevice`.

attributes.name: pressed
attributes.doc:
True while the pointer is down *and* this view was on the chain captured at pointer-down —
read-only. It stays true if the finger slides off and comes back, which is what makes a
button feel like a button; `hovered` alone flickers. The pair is the whole of press
styling: `fill = { pressed ? theme.line : hovered ? theme.control : null }`.

attributes.name: onScreen
attributes.doc:
Is this view **on screen** — inside the viewport, not scrolled away, not in a hidden
subtree? A coarse reactive fact that flips at threshold crossings, so a binding
re-derives only when the answer changes: the gate for ambient work
(`running = { classroot.onScreen && app.pageVisible }`) and for load culling. Fed
lazily at the first read — a program that never binds it pays nothing. On the DOM the
feed sees the whole page, so an embedded app's box scrolled off its **host** page
reads `false` too. Read-only.

(`running = { classroot.onScreen && app.pageVisible }`) and for load culling. Fed
lazily at the first read — a program that never binds it pays nothing. On the DOM the
feed sees the whole page, so an embedded app's box scrolled off its **host** page
reads `false` too. Read-only.

attributes.name: visibleRect
attributes.doc:
What of this view is visible, **in its own coordinates** — `{x, y, width, height}`,
all zeros when nothing shows. Updates **at rest** (when motion settles and scrolling
quiets), never per frame of a glide — a tile or rung decision wants the flight's end.
Cull margins are your arithmetic on the truth, not a platform knob. Read-only.

attributes.name: apparentScale
attributes.doc:
The composed scale from this view's units to **device pixels** — ancestor scales ×
devicePixelRatio. The raster-rung fact: an image pyramid picks its tier from it, a
drawn view its backing density, with no reimplemented transform math and no host
globals. Exact under Declare's own transforms (rotation does not participate); under
a non-similar host transform it is the largest axis ratio — the rasterization
convention. Same at-rest delivery as `visibleRect`. Read-only.

**The phase these facts have — and the one they don't.** All three answer *what is*,
at arrival: a camera flight lands, then a fact-bound tier re-derives, once. They never
answer *what will be* — the platform cannot know where a spring is headed, but **your
app can**, because the camera's target is your own attribute. A prefetch keyed on the
destination (`tierFor(cardH * app.camTarget)`) fires at departure and overlaps the
glide; a tier keyed on `apparentScale` asks on arrival and may land soft, then
sharpen. Those are opposite ends of the same flight, both legitimate: departure-phase
policy is written against your target state, arrival-phase truth against these facts,
and the two compose.

attributes.name: stroke
attributes.doc:
A border drawn **inside** the box (`stroke(width, color)`), so it never enlarges the
layout rectangle — the box stays the one geometry fact. `null` by default. Chosen over
CSS's `border` precisely so a bordered view and an unbordered one occupy the same space.

attributes.name: shadow
attributes.doc:
A drop shadow on the box (`shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`), the CSS box-shadow shape
minus spread. `null` by default. The glyph equivalent on `Text` is `textShadow`.

attributes.name: visible
attributes.doc:
Whether the view renders and participates in layout-that-skips-invisibles (default
`true`). A `false` view is fully inert — no paint, no hit-testing — but still
constructed, so toggling it is cheap and keeps its state.

attributes.name: ignoreLayout
attributes.doc:
Opt this child out of its parent's `layout` — the arrangement skips it and it owns
its own position on both axes (the decoration/overlay case: a badge floating over
a laid list). Its size still counts toward the parent's auto-extent.

attributes.name: ignoreClip
attributes.doc:
Opt this child out of its parent's `clip`: outside the parent's frame it still
paints *and* still hits — frame chrome that straddles the frame (a window's
resize halo; a badge poking out of a clipped card). Parent-scoped — an ancestor's
clip above still applies — and the child is exempt from the parent's auto-extent
(frame geometry derives *from* the bounds, so it cannot also define them).

attributes.name: ignoreScroll
attributes.doc:
The third member of the opt-out family (`ignoreLayout` — the parent arranges everyone
but me; `ignoreClip` — the parent clips everyone but me): **the scroll carries everyone
but me — I ride the frame.** The child stands still against its nearest enclosing scroll
frame — the window when the page is the regime, the pane's frame inside a `scrolls`
view — and contributes nothing to the scroll range. The fixed header, the pinned
toolbar, and the overlay layer that stages parked furniture are all this one attribute.

attributes.name: opacity
attributes.doc:
Whole-view alpha, `0`…`1` (default `1`). Applies to the view **and its subtree** as a
group, so a fading panel fades its contents with it. Not `prevailing`: its effect
already composes down the render tree, so a followed copy would apply it twice.

attributes.name: scale
attributes.doc:
A uniform transform — the view's subtree renders scaled about its pivot, and **every
reader agrees on the one geometry**: paint, hit-testing, `rootOrigin`, the parent's
auto-size, and layouts all compose the same transform, so a `scale = 0.5` child really
occupies half its slot (the fractal idiom) — where CSS makes transform paint-only and
lets layout disagree with what you see. The view's **own** `width`/`height` stay local
(its interior world is untouched — that is what makes scale mean "the same world,
smaller"); the parent packs the transformed **footprint** (`bounds()`). Pair with
`pivotX`/`pivotY` to choose the center; `1` is unscaled; spring it for zoom effects.

attributes.name: pivotX
attributes.doc:
The horizontal center of `scale` and `rotation`, in the view's own coordinates. Defaults
to the origin; set both `pivotX`/`pivotY` to transform about the middle rather than the
top-left.

docSegs.md:

to the origin; set both `pivotX`/`pivotY` to transform about the middle rather than the

attributes.name: pivotY
attributes.doc: The vertical pivot — the twin of `pivotX`.

docSegs.md: The vertical pivot — the twin of `pivotX`.

attributes.name: rotation
attributes.doc:
Rotation in **degrees**, clockwise, about the same (`pivotX`, `pivotY`) pivot `scale`
uses — and the same one-geometry rule: hit-testing follows the *visible* geometry
through the inverse transform (`hovered`, `pressed`, and `viewAt` all agree with what
you see), and layout and auto-size reserve the rotated frame's bounding box
(`bounds()`), so a rotated card takes the room it visibly covers. Composes with `scale`
in one documented order — scale, then rotate, about the shared pivot. `0` (the default)
is unrotated; spring it for turn effects.

attributes.name: blend
attributes.doc:
The **compositing operator** this view lands with against what has already painted
beneath it — `normal` (the default), or one of the W3C blend modes in camelCase
(`multiply`, `screen`, `overlay`, `darken`, `lighten`, `colorDodge`, `colorBurn`,
`hardLight`, `softLight`, `difference`, `exclusion`, `hue`, `saturation`, `color`,
`luminosity`, `plusLighter`). Declaration order — the z-order you already have — is
the blending order, and blending reaches down to the nearest **isolating** ancestor:
the `App` root, an `opacity < 1` group, a scrolling view's content, an island
boundary. A plain container is transparent to blending, so a `multiply` chip inside
nested layout Views blends against the card under them — which is what you meant.
A blending view blends **as a unit**, children included; compositing is paint, never
input — hit-testing and focus are unchanged. A token string in a `{ }` body, like
`scrolls` — so a blend can be state: `blend = { active ? "multiply" : "normal" }`.

attributes.type: normal | multiply | screen | overlay | darken | lighten | colorDodge | colorBurn | hardLight | softLight | difference | exclusion | hue | saturation | color | luminosity | plusLighter

attributes.name: backdrop
attributes.doc:
The **frost** — `frost(radius)` or `frost(radius, saturation)`; `null` (the default) =
none. What has already painted beneath this view is sampled within the view's **own
painted shape** (its box, rounded by `cornerRadius`, or its `clip` shape), blurred by
`radius`, saturation-scaled, and the view's own `fill` then paints **over** the frosted
sample — a translucent wash over a blurred backdrop, which is how every platform's
material works. Content moving beneath re-frosts; that is the point. Samples reach the
same isolating ancestor `blend` does, and like `blend` it is paint only — input never
changes. `saturation` defaults to `1`; frosted materials read best around `1.4`–`1.8`.

```declare
panel: View [ backdrop = frost(20), fill = #F9F9FBDB, cornerRadius = 12 ]
```

attributes.name: clip
attributes.doc:
Clips the subtree to a shape. `clip = true` clips to the view's **own box**
(reactively on width/height) — the common case; a `Shape` value clips to an arbitrary
path. `null`/unset (default) draws children unclipped, even outside the box. Kept
explicit (not implied by `cornerRadius`) so clipping is pay-per-use.

attributes.name: scrolls
attributes.doc:
Which **axes** of interior overflow this view scrolls — `none` (the default), `y`, `x`,
or `both`. One class overrides that default: an **`App` scrolls `y` by default**, and its
scroller is the page itself (the ruled page shape — see `App`). A scrolling view clips to its box; overflow along a declared axis becomes its
scroll range (live `scrollY`/`scrollX`), and overflow along any other axis is simply out
of frame. The value is a token **string** in a `{ }` body — compare explicitly
(`scrolls == "y"`), never truthily: `"none"` is a truthy string. Fixed chrome comes free — make it a **sibling** of the scroller, or a child that declares `ignoreScroll`.
Both backends present the same model; only the overscroll *feel* differs, where the
platform can do better. On DOM the OS owns the scroll — overlay scrollbar, momentum, and
rubber-band overscroll *contained* to this pane, so it bounces on its own edges and never
chains to the page, and sibling panes overscroll independently. On canvas the runtime
manages the offset (clip+translate+wheel), as a single element must.

attributes.name: claim
attributes.doc:
The axis a declared drag claims (`claim = x | y | both`, default `both`): `x` keeps
vertical pan with the enclosing scroll regime while the drag owns horizontal — a grid
column's header drag or edge-resize on touch. Scopes an existing drag declaration
(`onPointerMove`); it never creates one. See claim-surface.md for the arbitration.

attributes.name: tip
attributes.doc:
The tooltip text — the layer system's floor (one attribute at the use site): a non-empty
`tip` makes this view hover-interactive, and after the theme's delay the auto-provided
`Tooltip` singleton shows the text beside it. Placement, delay, and size are theme data
(`tooltipPlacement` below | above | pointer, `tooltipDelay`, `tooltipSize`) — so Cupertino
tips appear near the cursor after ~1s at 11px (the Cupertino help tag), Redmond's above the
control (WinUI), Mountain View's below at ~500ms (M3) — always flipped and clamped inside
the app. Moving between tip-carrying controls while a tip is up retargets instantly; a
press dismisses. Look comes from `tooltipBg` / `tooltipText` / `tooltipLine`. `""` (the
default) = no tip.

attributes.name: scrollY
attributes.doc:
The current vertical scroll offset in pixels of a `scrolls` view — the **platform writes
it** as the user scrolls; **read it** for scroll-driven effects (a fading header, reveals,
parallax): `opacity = { 1 - app.scrollY / 200 }`. To move the pane, **call `scrollTo(y)`**
rather than assigning: the verb is a request the platform clamps to the real range and
holds for a pane that cannot take it yet, where an assignment can be silently swallowed
(an equal-looking value, a hidden pane's lying offset). To reveal a particular view,
`scrollIntoView()` on the target already does the walk.

attributes.name: scrollX
attributes.doc:

from the native scroll — `scrollY`'s twin, with the enforcement `scrollY` still lacks:
the platform owns it, and assigning it is a compile error. **`scrollToX(x)` is the verb**
— a clamped, held request. A declared `Animator [ attribute = scrollX ]` may still drive
it (the sanctioned driver door — the desktop's Files strip animates a fresh column into
view). Read it for a paging strip's position or scroll-driven effects.

so **any** container can provide it and the whole subtree inherits, live. Unset, it
follows the nearest ancestor that sets it (default `0x000000`). Set it on a panel to
retint all text beneath without touching each `Text`.

with a generic. Prevailing, so setting it on a container refaces the whole region.

attributes.name: letterSpacing
attributes.doc:

attributes.name: iconSize
attributes.doc:
Prevailing icon size in pixels (default `16`), inherited exactly like `fontSize` and
`textColor`. A drawn icon takes its box from this, so setting it once on a container
sizes every mark in a region — a menu row asks for 16, a button for 18 — without each
icon carrying a number of its own.

It sizes the BOX, not the stroke: an icon's `weight` is in final pixels, so the same
mark at a larger `iconSize` reads proportionally lighter rather than simply scaling up.
That is deliberate — a hairline should stay a hairline — but it means a set drawn for
16 will not hold its density at 32 without redrawing.

attributes.doc:
A prevailing record of design tokens, read inside `{ }` as `theme.accent`, `theme.muted`,
etc. Provide it on a container and the subtree styles off it — the escape from hard-coded
colors when you don't want a full `stylesheet`.

attributes.name: selectable
attributes.doc:
Opt this run back into native text selection / copy (default `false`). Off by default
so an app doesn't feel like a document; turn it on for content a user should be able to
select and copy.

attributes.name: cursor
attributes.doc:
The pointer cursor shown over this view, as a CSS cursor keyword (`"col-resize"`,
`"grab"`); `""` inherits. This is how a resize edge or a drag handle announces itself
before anything is pressed. Meaningful on views that take input — the cursor follows the
hit target, so a view with `pointerEvents = "none"` never shows its own.

attributes.name: pointerEvents
attributes.doc:
Whether **this view** takes pointer events: `"auto"` (the default) or `"none"`.
`"none"` is for a view that is pure decoration over live content — a highlight rectangle,
a full-viewport chrome overlay — so presses reach what is beneath it. It is the fix for
the invisible-lid bug: an overlay sized to the frame that silently swallows every click.

It makes the view a **corridor, not a lid**: the press passes through this view, and each
child still answers for itself. A child carrying a handler keeps taking its own presses,
and a child may state `"auto"` outright — which is what lets a chrome overlay hold a real
panel (the Inspector's own window is exactly that) while the rest of it stays transparent.
So `"none"` on a container is not a way to disable a subtree; put it where the decoration
is, or gate the handlers.

attributes.name: styles
attributes.doc:
An ordered list of `style` bundles applied at **construction** — **static in v1**: unlike
`stylesheet`, reassigning `styles` after build does nothing. For a reskin that changes
live, use `stylesheet` instead.

docSegs.md:

live, use `stylesheet` instead.

attributes.name: stylesheet
attributes.doc:
Which declared sheet governs this subtree — **the attribute, not the top-level form of the
same name**. `stylesheet Dark [ … ]` DECLARES a skin; `stylesheet = Dark` APPLIES one. The
syntax tells them apart (a form is followed by a name, the attribute by `=`), and the shared
word is deliberate: it says what kind of thing `Dark` is.

Prevailing, so provide one anywhere and that whole subtree reskins; swap it and the subtree
re-styles in a single settle. A sheet is a dictionary keyed by CLASS name — no selectors, no
structural matching, no specificity — resolved by a class-chain walk with field-wise merge,
and its fields land as offers that sit BELOW any value the view sets itself. It carries a
`theme` record too, which is why a skin can be theme-aware.

The three styling channels differ by who decides: `styles` is opted into BY THE VIEW and is
static after construction; `theme` is a token record an ancestor provides and bindings READ;
a stylesheet is IMPOSED from outside on views that never mention it — style without source
edits.

attributes.name: layout
attributes.doc:
How this view arranges its children — a reactive `Layout` attribute, not a child and
not the container's type. Defaults to none (absolute `x`/`y`). Swap or animate it and
the arrangement transitions continuously: `layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ]`.
Set `layout = null` for explicit none.

attributes.name: datapath
attributes.doc:
The data cursor (language §9): sets the place in a dataset that this view and its
descendants read relative to. Write it as a `:path` (relative to the inherited
cursor), `:arr[]` to **replicate** this view once per array element, or a `{ }`
expression yielding a place. Descendants read with their own relative `:paths`.

attributes.name: focusable
attributes.doc:
Makes the view a keyboard **tab stop**. Traversal order is the view tree — there is no
numeric tabindex; override `tabOrder()` to reorder within a container.

attributes.name: focusTrap
attributes.doc:
Marks a self-contained focus group: Tab cycles within it and escapes at the boundary
(firing `escapeFocus`). For a modal or menu whose focus must not leak to the page behind.

attributes.name: anchor
attributes.doc:
Names this view as a **reveal target** for a location's `@name` suffix
(`#guide/04-tree@intro` scrolls to the view with `anchor = "intro"`). The `<a name>`
lineage, reborn reactive: the anchor namespace is named views (this attribute) plus
heading slugs inside rendered rich text — a heading needs nothing from you. Resolution
prefers views over slugs, preorder-first.

attributes.name: contentWidth
attributes.doc:
**Read-only** intrinsic: the width of this view's visible children's bounding box —
the auto-extent, surfaced. A constraint may read it (`width = { Math.min(contentWidth, 480) }`)
to size to content with a cap; assigning it is a compile error.

the auto-extent, surfaced. A constraint may read it (`width = { Math.min(contentWidth, 480) }`)
to size to content with a cap; assigning it is a compile error.

attributes.name: childViews
attributes.doc:
This view's child views, as a live collection — reading it re-runs when the child **set**
changes. It carries set membership only, not the children's own attributes: `.length` is
live, but `.map(c => c.width)` would wire half of what it reads, so aggregation over a node
collection is refused rather than answered wrongly.

**On a virtualized block it answers with the instances that exist** — a subset of the
records, and it changes as you scroll. That is a fact about the block, not a trap: check
`virtualized` on this same container and you know which kind of answer you are holding
(the flag is declared on the replicated child, but read on the container — see
`virtualized`). The list also includes instances the recycler has parked
(`visible = false`), because they are children.

**For a count of the collection, count the data.** The records are complete by definition;
the instances never claimed to be.

```declare-fragment
count: number = { (app.d.value.rows).length }
```

If you want the window with its logical indices — an accessibility traversal, a diagnostic
— that is kernel API (`blocksOf`, `realized()`, `materializationInfo`).

attributes.name: virtualized
attributes.doc:
Whether **this view's replicated content** is virtualized right now — a content intrinsic,
like `contentWidth` and `contentHeight`, and read-only. `false` unless this view is the
container of a virtualized block, which is every view in a program that never asks for
virtualization.

**Read it on the CONTAINER, not the template.** `virtualize` is declared on the replicated
child — beside its `datapath = :rows[]`, where `key` lives too — but the block belongs to
the *parent* that holds the instances, so the parent is what answers. A row instance reports
`false`, and that is the honest answer: an instance has no replicated content of its own. In
ordinary speech the list is virtualized, not the row.

```declare-fragment
list: View [ datapath = { app.d.value },                  // ← ask THIS one
    Row [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ]         // ← declared HERE
    ]
```

It is **tracked**, so a constraint reading it follows a block engaging or disengaging —
which can happen mid-run, since the policy accepts a `{ }`. And it is what makes
`childViews` legible on a virtualized block: the list is a subset, and this is how you know.

attributes.name: virtualize
attributes.doc:
Virtualize this replicated collection: build the instances near the viewport and leave the
rest logical, reconstructed indistinguishably as you scroll. **Replication metadata** — it
belongs on the node whose `datapath` matches many, beside that path, and it means nothing
anywhere else (a node that replicates nothing has no collection to describe, and the checker
says so).

**A boolean, off by default.** Below the threshold where construction hurts, materializing
everything is simply faster and keeps `childViews` whole; above it, this is the one word that
changes. There is no automatic mode and no count to tune — a virtualized block costs a flat
~0.06 ms per scroll tick at any size, so there is no cliff a threshold could protect, and
what full materialization actually costs is construction, which depends on how rich a row is
rather than how many there are.

Like any boolean it takes a `{ }`, and the policy is read inside the replication match — so a
collection can start fully materialized and virtualize when it grows, engaging and
disengaging as the answer changes. What you never write is everything *around* the word: no
row heights, no scroll container, no keys, no overscan tuning, no memoization.

Virtualization needs a scrolling ancestor (`scrolls = y`, or `both`) and — if the block's
parent runs a layout — that layout must stack on `y`. A wrapping gallery, a horizontal strip,
a scatter of pins: those fully materialize instead, deliberately, with an inspectable reason.
Read `virtualized` on the container to see whether it engaged.

```declare-fragment
Row [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ]
```

attributes.name: contentHeight
attributes.doc:
**Read-only** intrinsic mirroring `contentWidth` on the vertical axis — the measured
extent of the subtree, for sizing a container to its content.

docSegs.md:

events.name: click
hold
events.doc:
A press held in place for half a second — the tap-hold, equally available to a mouse.
It does **not** consume the gesture: the raw stream continues and the eventual click
still fires unless the pointer wanders, so a hold can open a menu, start a pick-up, or
be ignored. Declared **alongside the drag handlers** it changes who owns a touch
finger: the drag's claim engages *at the hold* instead of at touchdown, so a quick
swipe still scrolls the surface underneath and a held finger picks the thing up — the
hold-to-drag idiom for draggables on scrolling surfaces.

events.name: pointerDown
events.doc:
The pointer pressed on the view — the raw press phase. Prefer `click` (press **and**
release on the same view) unless you need the phases apart, e.g. to begin a drag.

docSegs.md:
The pointer pressed on the view — the raw press phase. Prefer `click` (press **and**
release on the same view) unless you need the phases apart, e.g. to begin a drag.

events.name: pointerUp
events.doc:
The pointer released. While a press is captured (it began on this view) `pointerUp` still
fires **here even if the release lands off the box** — the drag-release guarantee, so a
slider freezes its value wherever the finger lifts.

fires **here even if the release lands off the box** — the drag-release guarantee, so a
slider freezes its value wherever the finger lifts.

events.name: pointerMove
events.doc:
The pointer moved over the view — and, once pressed on it, every move **while captured**
(even outside the box), so a drag handler keeps getting positions. The event carries the
pointer in this view's own coordinates.

docSegs.md:
The pointer moved over the view — and, once pressed on it, every move **while captured**
(even outside the box), so a drag handler keeps getting positions. The event carries the
pointer in this view's own coordinates.

events.name: pointerOver
events.doc:
The pointer entered the view (retained enter tracking) — the hover-in half. Set a
`hovered` flag here and read it in a `fill`/`textColor` constraint.

docSegs.md:
The pointer entered the view (retained enter tracking) — the hover-in half. Set a
`hovered` flag here and read it in a `fill`/`textColor` constraint.

events.name: pointerOut
events.doc:
The pointer left the view — the hover-out half; also fires when a press is abandoned off
the box, so clear both `hovered` and `pressed` here.

docSegs.md:
The pointer left the view — the hover-out half; also fires when a press is abandoned off
the box, so clear both `hovered` and `pressed` here.

events.name: wheel
events.doc:
The wheel turned over the view — mouse wheel, trackpad scroll, or trackpad pinch, which
arrives on the same stream with `e.pinch` true (a ctrl+wheel zoom reports identically).
The event carries the point in this view's coordinates plus `deltaX`/`deltaY`. Declaring
it **claims the wheel** over this view and its subtree — the browser stops scrolling or
zooming the page with it — except over a nested `scrolls` pane, which keeps its own
wheel. ⌘ +/− dispatches no event and stays out of reach.

events.name: pinchStart
events.doc:
Two fingers landed over this view's subtree — the **recognized** two-finger gesture,
so you never do the finger arithmetic (that is what the raw `onTouch*` family is for).
Declaring any of the pinch family **claims the two-finger gesture** from the browser
over this subtree; single-finger pan stays the enclosing regime's — the same
narrowing `claim = x` performs for drags. The event carries `scale` (`1` at the
start) and `center`, the midpoint of the two fingers in root space. A pinch nearly
always drives `scale`/`rotation` of a sub-surface, which is why they ship together.

events.name: pinch
events.doc:
The fingers moved: `e.scale` is **cumulative** — the spread now over the spread at
`pinchStart` — and `e.center` tracks the midpoint in root space. Typical use:
`onPinch(e) { zoom = anchor * e.scale }`, anchoring on the value at `pinchStart`
rather than integrating deltas.

events.name: pinchEnd
events.doc:
Either finger lifted (or the browser reclaimed the gesture); `e.scale` is the final
cumulative scale. Latch your anchor here for the next pinch.

events.name: retire
events.doc:
The departure hook — fires once when this view's PRESENCE ends (its record leaves the
replicated match, or the subtree is discarded), children before parents, with everything
still alive. The exact symmetric of `onInit`'s membership rule: a windowed row's
dematerialization is NOT a departure and never fires it.

events.name: focus
events.doc:
The view gained keyboard focus (it is `focusable` and was tabbed or clicked to). Drive a
focus ring off it.

events.doc: The view lost keyboard focus — the partner of `focus`.

events.name: escapeFocus
events.doc:
Fired on a `focusTrap` when Tab reaches its boundary — your cue to move focus out (close

events.name: keyDown
events.doc:
A key was pressed while the view holds focus; the event carries the key. For app-wide
shortcuts use a `Keys` subscription instead — this is for the focused view only.

methods.name: removeChild
methods.doc:
Detaches a child from this view. The child is **not** torn down — use `discard()` for
that; a removed view you keep a reference to can be inserted somewhere else.

methods.name: insertChild
methods.doc:
Inserts a view you already hold as a child at `index` — the placement primitive beneath
`createView`. Prefer replication over data for collections; this is for genuinely
imperative structure. A primitive, not a verb: it does not notify the arrangement — after
imperative re-ordering, the layout re-packs on the next arrival or removal.
