tree.name: Tip
tree.doc:
The tooltip service, as a member: `onTip(e)` fires when a view carrying `tip = "…"` wants
its tooltip shown, and with `null` when it should hide. The service owns the platform
conventions — the show delay, instant retarget while showing, hide on press — so a
listener only renders.

The library's `Tooltip` is the one listener most programs ever need, and it arrives
automatically in any app whose views carry tips. Declare your own `Tip [ … ]` member only
when you are replacing that rendition.

```declare-fragment
tips: Tip [
    onTip(e: TipEvent) {
        if (e == null) { classroot.shown = false; return }
        classroot.label = e.text
        classroot.shown = true
        }
    ]
```

tree.name: Stream
tree.doc:
The abstract base of the live-connection sources — `EventStream` (SSE) and `Socket`
(WebSocket) extend it. Not instantiable: write the concrete transport. The one thing to
know: **there is no `connect()` or `disconnect()`** — the declaration decides. A stream is
connected exactly while `active` is true and `url` is non-empty; empty the url (or flip
`active`) and it closes, change the url and it closes and reopens, remove the node and the
connection dies with it. Nothing to unsubscribe, ever. Messages are **transient**: nothing
accumulates unless a handler writes it somewhere — the runtime keeps only `last`. An app
that streams JSON parses in the handler (`JSON.parse(e.data)`) and writes wherever it
wants; accumulation is one line of app code, deliberately not a built-in policy.

```declare-fragment
chat: View [
    answer: string = "",
    reply: EventStream [ url = { `/api/chat?id=${classroot.chatId}` },
        active = { classroot.chatId != "" },
        onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { classroot.answer = classroot.answer + e.data },
        ],
    out: Text [ width = { parent.width }, text = { parent.answer } ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: url
attributes.doc:
Where to connect — a literal or a `{ }` constraint. Unlike `DataSource.url`, a change acts
**immediately**: the old connection closes and a new one opens at the new address (there is
no fetch() moment to wait for). `""` means detached — the idiom for "no conversation yet"
is deriving emptiness: `url = { app.chatId != "" ? "/api/chat/" + app.chatId : "" }`.

attributes.name: active
attributes.doc:
The gate. `false` closes the connection (and cancels any pending retry); flipping back
`true` reopens it. Bind it to app state — `active = { app.live }` — rather than toggling
imperatively.

docSegs.md:

attributes.name: retry
attributes.doc:
Reconnect policy, **visible in the declaration**: seconds to wait before re-dialing after
the connection is lost and the platform won't bring it back on its own — a `Socket`'s
unexpected close, an `EventStream`'s terminal failure. `0` (the default) means no retry:
the stream lands in `status = "failed"` and the app decides. A declared retry keeps trying
while `active` is true, at a **fixed** interval — no invisible backoff, no give-up count.
A structural failure (the factory itself refuses — headless extraction, a missing host
service) never loops, whatever `retry` says.

attributes.name: status
attributes.doc:
The connection lifecycle as **one fact**, like `DataSource.status`: `"closed"`,
`"connecting"`, `"open"`, `"retrying"`, or `"failed"` (down, and will not reconnect).
**Read-only** — computed for you; assigning it is a compile error. `"retrying"` covers
both the platform's own recovery (SSE) and a declared `retry` waiting to re-dial.

yourself if it is JSON, concatenate it if it is streamed text; the runtime never guesses.

`e.id` is the SSE last-event-id (`""` on sockets).

Prefer deriving from `open`/`status` for anything a constraint can express; the handler is
for work state cannot do (send a subscription frame, log).

events.doc:

removal at discard is silent), the server ended it, or it failed. Fires once per
connection, before any retry dials the next one.

that is not open. The reason is in `error` when the handler runs. The platform's own
in-flight retries (SSE) are **not** errors and stay quiet.

tree.name: EventStream
tree.doc:
Server-Sent Events (`text/event-stream`) as a source — the streaming-AI shape: the server
pushes, the app receives, an `onMessage` that concatenates is the whole consumer. See
`Stream` for the shared surface (`url`/`active`/`retry`, the read-only
`status`/`open`/`error`/`last`). Receive-only — there is no `send`; a request that needs a
body is an ordinary `DataSource` POST, and the stream carries the reply. The platform's
`EventSource` machinery is kept **verbatim**: it retries on its own (honoring the server's
`retry:` hint) and resumes with `Last-Event-ID`, during which `status` reads `"retrying"`
and no error is reported; `retry`/`onError` concern only **terminal** failure — the
platform giving up.

A declared stream **holds a live connection** for as long as it is `active` and its node
lives — every open tab is one held server connection (browsers cap ~6 per host over
HTTP/1.1, so a dev server's tabs can exhaust the pool). The lifecycle is the declaration:
`active = { app.chatId != "" }` releases the connection the moment the condition goes
false, and a discarded node closes its own — there is nothing to unsubscribe.

```declare-fragment
answer: string = "",
reply: EventStream [ url = { `/api/chat?id=${app.chatId}` },
    active = { app.chatId != "" },
    onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.answer = app.answer + e.data },
    ]
```

attributes.name: listenTo
attributes.doc:
The **named** SSE event types to deliver — `listenTo = ["content_block_delta",
"message_stop"]`. Required for any stream that labels messages with `event:` lines
(Anthropic-style AI streams do): the platform's `EventSource` physically cannot deliver a
named event it was not asked to listen for, so an undeclared name is silently invisible —
if `onMessage` sees nothing but the connection is `open`, this is the first thing to
check. The name carries the contract: you hear what you listen to. Unnamed (default)
messages always arrive; `e.type` says which kind each one is.

tree.name: Socket
tree.doc:
WebSocket as a source: the `Stream` surface plus `send(text)` — `send` is a call you make,
`onMessage` is it calling you. See `Stream` for `url`/`active`/`retry` and the read-only
`status`/`open`/`error`/`last`. Unlike SSE the platform has **no native reconnect**, so a
`Socket` that should survive a dropped connection must say so: `retry = 2` re-dials two
seconds after any close the app didn't ask for, for as long as `active` holds — the whole
policy is that one number. Text frames only; a binary frame is dropped (a later attribute
if a real project needs one, not a speculative shape now).

```declare-fragment
live: Socket [ url = "wss://api.example.com/feed", retry = 2,
    onOpen() { this.send('{"subscribe":"prices"}') },
    onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.tick(JSON.parse(e.data)) },
    ]
```

methods.name: send
methods.doc:
Sends one text frame. **Legal only while `open`** — on a socket that is not open it sends
nothing and reports through the error channel (`error` + `onError`), never a silent queue:
if the app needs buffering-until-connected, that policy belongs in app state, visibly.
Sending the opening frame belongs in `onOpen` (which also covers every reconnect); gate
user-triggered sends on `.open`.

tree.name: State
tree.doc:
A named bundle of overrides that snaps on and off **together**. Its body is not ordinary
children: a `name = value` entry is an **override of the enclosing view's own attribute**
(checked against *that* view's schema, not the State's), applied while the state is on;
an `id: Type [ … ]` entry is a conditional subtree that exists only while applied. Because
attribute reads compose as a **precedence stack**, the base values return *exactly* when
the state turns off — there is no manual undo to write, and no drift.

```declare
card: View [ height = 72, fill = white,
    open: State [ applied = { expanded }, height = 184, fill = lightsteelblue,
        Text [ text = "shown only while open" ]
        ]
    ]
```

an `id: Type [ … ]` entry is a conditional subtree that exists only while applied. Because

```declare

    open: State [ applied = { expanded }, height = 184, fill = lightsteelblue,
        Text [ text = "shown only while open" ]
        ]

```

attributes.name: applied
attributes.doc:
Whether the state is on. Bind it to a condition (`applied = { expanded }`) and the whole
bundle snaps in and out as that flips — the base values restore themselves when it turns
off. The declarative alternative to the `apply()` / `remove()` / `toggle()` verbs.

Fires when the bundle turns **on** — after the overrides compose onto the stack, so reads
in the handler already see the state's values. Use for a side effect that must ride with the
state (focus a revealed field), not to mutate what the state already declares.

example.source:
App [ fill = white, textColor = black,
    open: boolean = false,
    onClick() { open = !open },
    card: View [ x = 30, y = 30, width = 300, height = 70,
        cornerRadius = 10, fill = whitesmoke,
        Text [ x = 20, y = 20, fontWeight = bold, text = "Summary" ],
        big: State [ applied = { open }, height = 180, fill = lightsteelblue,
            Text [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 260, wrap = true,
                text = "height, color, and this whole line swap in together" ]
            ]
        ]

tree.name: Node
tree.doc:
The plain object-graph atom — a **non-visual** node you subclass for logic that isn't a
view: a controller, a coordinator, a service. A bare `class X [ … ]` **defaults its base to
`Node`**, so a class with attributes and methods but no box *is* a Node subclass. It lives in
the tree as a named member, shares the reactive core and the `classroot`/`app` reach, and
fires `init` — but it paints nothing. Reach for it instead of a View when a wrapper class
would be visual in name only.

```declare
class Cart [ count: number = 0,
    add()    { count = count + 1 },
    clear()  { count = 0 }
    ]
```

A view then holds one as a named member (`cart: Cart [ ]`) and reads/drives it reactively —
state and behaviour with no pixels of its own.

```declare
class Cart [ count: number = 0,
    add()    { count = count + 1 },
    clear()  { count = 0 }
    ]
```

A view then holds one as a named member (`cart: Cart [ ]`) and reads/drives it reactively —
state and behaviour with no pixels of its own.

(the init walk covers non-View children since 2026-08-20 — before that, only views were
visited and a Node's `onInit` silently never fired). Answered by `onInit()`.

tree.name: Bar
tree.doc:
A labeled horizontal value bar: an optional caption, then a rounded track filled to
`value`. A **placeholder component** (composition.md §1a) — coherent and restyleable,
but not the final widget. For a themed, theme-tracking meter reach for `ProgressBar`
instead; `Bar` exists for demos and dashboards that want a caption and their own colour.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    Bar [ width = 260, label = "Storage", value = 72 ],
    Bar [ width = 260, label = "Memory",  value = 38, tint = #37E0C8 ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Control
tree.doc:
The interaction-state base every stateful control extends (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md,
Contract 3). It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and
nothing semantic: `checked`, `value`, and their kin live on the concrete control.

The pointer half is the language's now: `hovered` and `pressed` are View's read-only
interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is
the CONTROL policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads:

- `hot` / `down` — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by `disabled`, with the
  keyboard-activation `flash` folded into `down`. Style against these, not the raw
  intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up.
- `disabled` — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it.
- keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same `press()`
  path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look.

It also owns the two things every labelled control was improvising:

- `iconLeft` / `iconRight` — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays
  them out; Control only declares that they exist, so `Button` and `Segment`
  answer to one vocabulary.
- `menu` — the ROLE of dropping a menu. Not decoration: fifteen sites across the
  corpus call `someMenu.openFor(control)`, and the disclosure mark for that one
  role was drawn five different ways or omitted (a glyph inside the label string
  in five places, a private chevron in two, a separate `Text` in one, nothing in
  `MenuBar` and `DataGrid`). Nobody chose those differences. Setting `menu` gets
  the mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and Down-to-open together,
  which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong one piece at a time.

Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated,
and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships:

```declare
class Stepper extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6,
    n: number = 0,
    fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control },
    press() { n = n + 1 },
    onClick() { if (!disabled) press() },
    t: Text [ x = center, y = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ]
    ]


App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]
```

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.doc:
Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into `hot`/`down` so a
disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `theme.disabledOpacity`.

disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `theme.disabledOpacity`.

attributes.name: focused
attributes.doc:
True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the *ring*, you want nothing: the
app-level `FocusRing` indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own
focus styling.

attributes.name: hot
attributes.doc:
Hover under control policy — `hovered` gated by `disabled`. **Style against this, not
the raw `hovered` intrinsic**, or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always
false on touch, since `hovered` is.

attributes.name: down
attributes.doc:
The pressed look — the `pressed` intrinsic gated by `disabled`, **with keyboard
activation folded in**, so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press
gives. The other half of the styling pair with `hot`.

attributes.name: focusVisible
attributes.doc:
Focused **and** the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's `:focus-visible` channel.
Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no
keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a `Pane` header's focus edge reads.

attributes.name: iconLeft
attributes.doc:
A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it.

attributes.doc:

chevron a `menu` would imply** — see `rightIcon`.

attributes.name: menu
attributes.doc:
The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (`menu = { app.optionsMenu }`).
Setting it is a *role*, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below
the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. **Declare
one menu and point many controls at it** rather than one per opener; the menu reads
`opener` to vary its items.

attributes.doc:

written** — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way
(Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open
look forever.

is the pointer's truth and is read-only. Folded into `down`, so styling needs to read

events.name: focus
events.doc:
Records focus and captures the keyboard modality into `focusVisible`. An override must
keep both or the focus channel goes dark.

events.name: pointerDown
events.doc:
Claims focus, clears the `:focus-visible` channel, and opens `menu` if there is one —
menus open on **press**, not release, as the platform does. **An override must keep the
`Focus.focus(this)` call**, or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere.

methods.doc:
Opens `menu` anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled.
The seam a concrete control calls from its own `press()`.

methods.doc:
**The activation seam — override this, not the handlers.** Pointer and keyboard both
land here, so one override serves a click, Space, and Enter. The base opens `menu` when
there is one. A value control delivers through `input` from here and **never writes its
own value slot directly**, which is what lets a bound control avoid fighting its
constraint.

methods.name: focusShape
methods.doc:
The focus silhouette the ring hugs, `{ x, y, w, h, rad }` in this control's own
coordinates. `null` (the default) rings the whole bounds at its `cornerRadius`. Override
to ring the part that means something — a `Radio` rings its dot, a `Slider` its thumb.

methods.name: flashPress
methods.doc:
Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention
for buttons and menu items. **Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback
(Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it.**

tree.name: Checkbox
tree.doc:
A boolean control (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1). Its value is the
`checked` attribute; **`input` owns the value's destination** — by default the
destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring:

    mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ]          … visible = { mute.checked }

Hand the value to its real owner by overriding `input` and constraining down:

    Checkbox [ label = "Mute", checked = { app.muted }, input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v } ]

`press()` never writes `checked` directly — it only delivers — so a bound checkbox
never fights its constraint.

```declare
row: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ],
    Text [ text = { mute.checked ? "muted" : "audible" } ]
    ]
```

destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring:

never fights its constraint.

App [

        ]

attributes.name: checked
attributes.doc:
Whether the box is ticked. Standalone it owns this and you read it back by name; bound
(`checked = { app.muted }`) it needs an `input` override to go with it — **a one-way
binding with no `input` leaves the checkbox's own edit assigning to a constrained slot,
which is refused at runtime.**

This is the one member to override when the value lives elsewhere.

methods.doc:

tree.name: Button
tree.doc:
A labeled action control. The action is its `onClick` — write it at the use site
exactly as on any View; `Button` adds the interaction states, the themed look, and
keyboard activation (Space/Enter drives the same `onClick`). `primary = true` fills
with the accent; the default is the quiet control look.

```declare-fragment
Button [ label = "Save" ]
Button [ label = "Delete", iconLeft = "TrashIcon" ]
Button [ label = "Options", menu = { app.optionsMenu } ]      // chevron implied
Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ]                             // icon only
```

Three slots in a row — `iconLeft`, the label, `iconRight` — laid out by
`SimpleLayout` and sized from `contentWidth`, so an absent label or icon costs
nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space
reclaimed. A `menu` supplies the right icon on its own (`control.declare`).

The fill walks the four-rung ladder — `control` at rest, `controlHover`,
`controlPressed`, and `controlSelected` while its menu is open. Before the ladder
existed this read `down || hot ? controlActive : control`, which meant **hovering
a button looked exactly like pressing it**.

tree.name: Slider
tree.doc:
A bounded number by drag (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md, Contract 1). Same value
contract as every control — `value` is the attribute, **`input` owns the
destination** (default: itself) — and the delivery is CONTINUOUS during a drag
(ruled: the owner decides what to do with the stream; the data layer owns
coalescing). Pressing the track jumps to that position (local coordinates);
the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta (`app.pointerX` — the
captured-move pattern the calendar's drag uses). Arrow keys nudge by `step`.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
    vol: Slider [ value = 40 ],
    Text [ text = { `volume ${Math.round(vol.value)}` } ]
    ]
```

(its DIRECT child, arranged by the row's layout):

concrete evidence for that item's priority.

tree.name: FocusRing
tree.doc:
The traveling focus indicator — the OpenLaszlo 3.4 `focusoverlay` line, on the
reactive core, at its third form: a SHAPE-HUGGING rounded outline whose
terminus reshapes to the focused control's own silhouette (library-charter §6
— the ring springs position, size, AND cornerRadius; a Radio's row ring, a
pill Switch's ring, and a text field's ring differ because the targets do).

The layered model (charter, ratified):

- **The fact** — the ring listens to Focus (a `Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { … } ]` member) and
  tracks the target's root-space geometry on EVERY change, pointer or
  keyboard. A pointer focus PARKS the ring there silently (snap, no show) —
  so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked,
  never from a stale perch.
- **Roles, theme-elected** — `theme.focusRing`: `"both"` (or `true`, the
  default) · `"travel"` (flight + the OL idle fade) · `"rest"` (no flight —
  the ring appears in place and stays) · `false` (no ring; the theme's
  components carry the at-rest indication — the invariant lives with the
  THEME+components pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role includes
  rest, the ring RESTS — no idle fade; a pointer press clears modality and
  the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics).
- **The flight is the flourish** — `theme.focusAnimate = false` (the
  sampler's "Animate focus transitions" toggle) snaps every move; the
  underdamped travel is default-on.

It arrives automatically with any Control-descended component (the OL
`canvas.focusclass` default); declare your own `FocusRing [ ]` (or subclass)
to replace it. Pure chrome: never focusable, never a pointer target.
(v1 limits, recorded: root-space bounds are summed through the parent chain —
a scrolled container is not compensated; the silhouette is the target's
`cornerRadius` — a `focusShape()` override protocol arrives with the
emulation passes.)

**You do not instantiate this, and you do not position it.** Tab between the controls
below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition,
and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour.

```declare
row: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ],
    Button [ label = "One" ],
    Button [ label = "Two" ],
    Checkbox [ label = "Three" ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Accordion
tree.doc:
OpenLaszlo's `basetabslider`, reborn — stacked pane headers, one
pane open at a time, panes SLIDING open and closed by a spring on height. The
load-bearing mechanic (docs/system-design/tabslider-gaps.md, verified
frame-by-frame against the original): a pane's content is PRESENT through the
whole open **and** close, revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its
height animates — never an instant pop, never a blank gap.

Value contract (components-baseline.md): the open pane is ONE attribute on the
group — `value`, the open pane's name — exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are
the group's direct children; each names itself (`name`, defaulting to its
`label`) and derives `open` from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's
ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips.

```declare
Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true,
        Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, wrap = true,
            text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ]
        ],
    Pane [ label = "Privacy",
        Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, text = "One pane open at a time." ]
        ]
    ]
```

invariant cannot break.

Assign it to open a pane from code; `""` closes all of them. A `Pane` never stores
whether it is open, it derives it from here, which is why the one-open-at-a-time
invariant cannot break.

tree.name: Pane
tree.doc:
OpenLaszlo's `basetabslider`, reborn — stacked pane headers, one
pane open at a time, panes SLIDING open and closed by a spring on height. The
load-bearing mechanic (docs/system-design/tabslider-gaps.md, verified
frame-by-frame against the original): a pane's content is PRESENT through the
whole open **and** close, revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its
height animates — never an instant pop, never a blank gap.

Value contract (components-baseline.md): the open pane is ONE attribute on the
group — `value`, the open pane's name — exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are
the group's direct children; each names itself (`name`, defaulting to its
`label`) and derives `open` from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's
ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips.

```declare
Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true,
        Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, wrap = true,
            text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ]
        ],
    Pane [ label = "Privacy",
        Text [ x = 12, y = 8, width = 230, text = "One pane open at a time." ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Tooltip
tree.doc:
The layer system's floor (planes.md §2, tier 1): any view sets `tip = "…"`
and this singleton renders it — hover delay, placement, flip, and theming
are nobody's problem at the use site. It arrives automatically when any
view in the program carries a tip (the FocusRing auto-arrival mechanism);
declare your own `Tooltip [ ]` (or subclass) to replace the rendition.

It listens to the Tip service (a `Tip [ onTip(e: TipEvent) { … } ]` member), which owns the platform
conventions (the show delay — `tooltipDelay`, ~1s in the Cupertino and Redmond
conventions, ~500ms Material — instant retarget while showing, hide on
press). PLACEMENT is theme data too (`tooltipPlacement`): "below" (the
default — under the target, centered, flipping above at the edge), "above"
(Fluent/WinUI's default, flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag —
offset below-right of where the cursor rests). Always clamped inside the
app. Pure chrome — never focusable, never a pointer target, always above
content (the auto-splice puts it last in the App, and source order stacks).

Theming (the four cities carry the tokens): `tooltipBg` / `tooltipText` /
`tooltipLine` (null = no border) / `tooltipSize` (11 in Cupertino, 12
elsewhere). Cupertino and Redmond wear bordered surface chips; San
Francisco and Mountain View the inverse chip.

**You do not instantiate this.** Set `tip` on any view and the singleton appears; the
members below exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition.

```declare
View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 130, height = 38, cornerRadius = 8, fill = steelblue,
    tip = "Saves your changes",
    Text [ x = center, y = center, textColor = white, text = "Save" ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Menu
tree.doc:
The record-driven menu (planes.md §4–§6): items are DATA — the component
arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS
menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }

- `key` renders right-aligned (display only — registration is the Keys
  service's, later).
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.

  This was THREE mechanisms before the icon set landed: a text glyph (`"◐"`), a
  hardcoded `"lightbulb"` that special-cased its way to a drawn bulb because no
  glyph matched, and `iconKind` naming a class. The middle one was the tell —
  somebody needed a mark the fonts could not give, and the escape hatch already
  existed. One field now; a COMPUTED name needs its class kept with
  `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow; the cascade itself
  lands with the roving-keyboard stage).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's CONTENT with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.

Declared ONCE, opened by many (the worked example): rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
RAISE the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app.

Dismissal: the BACKDROP (a full-app child under the panel) — a press
outside closes AND is swallowed, the Mac rule (planes.md §12.1, resolved
for v1); Escape closes; pick closes after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: items
attributes.doc:
The rows, as **records — never children**. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it
views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is
`{ id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }`;
a plain array is fine (no `Dataset` required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it
can be a constraint — **derive it from `opener` and one menu serves every row of a
table**, live while it is open.

attributes.name: opener
attributes.doc:

**The key to declaring one menu and opening it from many places**: read it in the
`items` constraint to vary the rows per opener, with no per-opener instance.

tree.name: MenuBar
tree.doc:
The record-driven menu bar (planes.md §4–§6): whole menus are DATA —

    menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] }

— and the component arranges. ONE internal Menu serves every title; its
`items` constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state
(enabled, checked, labels) stays LIVE while the menu is up. Because the
records are the single declaration, an app can derive its key registry
from the same array the bar renders — nothing is declared twice (the
Newton keys direction, proven in apps/desktop).

Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do NOT highlight on mere hover;
a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving
across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes.

Delivery is the one seam: `picked(id)` — override at the use site.

```declare
App [ width = 380, height = 120, chose: string = "",
    bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8,
        menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }),
                                                          ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }),
                    ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }),
                                                           ({ divider: true }),
                                                           ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Dialog
tree.doc:
The modal tier (planes.md): a full-app SCRIM that swallows every press —
modal input blocking, no light dismiss — under a centered panel with a
focusTrap. Buttons are RECORDS (the records door): `{ id, label,
default?, cancel? }`, rendered as themed library Buttons right-aligned in
the platform arrangement. Focus SAVES on open and RETURNS on close.

Keyboard: Return picks the DEFAULT button (the Cupertino rule; a focused
button also activates on Space/Enter — the pick guard makes the double
harmless), Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just
closes.

The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id
(the `picked(id)` override remains the declarative seam):

    dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.")
    dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …)
    dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.")

`ask` is Cancel / No / Yes-default; `error` renders the title in the
theme's errorColor.

Platform STRUCTURE is data (the scheme): `dialogWidth`,
`dialogButtons` = "end" (a right-aligned row — SF, Material) | "stack"
(the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, DEFAULT ON TOP) | "fill"
(WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row),
`dialogAlign` = "left" | "center" (the Cupertino centered title),
`dialogTitleSize` / `dialogBodySize`. Plus scrimColor + scrimOpacity
(Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by SHADOW; Material's spec scrim is
32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, errorColor.

**Declare one and call it.** A `Dialog` is not a view you show and hide around your
content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves
every prompt in the program.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 140, said: string = "",
    dlg: Dialog [ ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…",
        onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.",
                                (id) => { app.said = id }) }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: AppIsland
tree.doc:
`AppIsland` embeds a live Declare application: give it a `program` and it mounts
that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and
stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills
the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view.

It composes `DOMIsland` (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the
host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the
`run:…` wire. The page host (`browser/host-client.js`) sees the key on the box,
resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile,
identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child.

`childName` (inherited from `DOMIsland`) is the reverse channel: the running child's
`appName` reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

attributes.name: program
attributes.doc:
What to run: a program name, a relative path (`"../../calendar/calendar"` reaches the
real app — **no copy of the source, ever**), or the reserved `"__raw__"` live-edit
channel, where the running program is the host app's `liveSource` and recompiles as it
changes. **`""` detaches the island** and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel
stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a
view of itself.

tree.name: SimpleLayout
tree.doc:
The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

across a row with the ordinary `y = center`. Override it in a subclass for custom

tree.name: WrappingLayout
tree.doc:
A horizontal flow that WRAPS: children run left to right
`spacing` apart, and when the next one would overflow the view's width it
drops to a new row (`lineSpacing` down; -1, the default, means "same as
spacing"). With room for one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it
stacks — cards that reflow on a phone with no media query. It owns BOTH
axes of each child (a flow is 2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `align`
justifies each finished row: `start` (left, the default) or `center` (a row
that does not fill the width sits centered).

Division of labor: this is the tool for UNIFORM, replicated collections
that reflow by fitting. Managing NAMED regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
    ]
```

both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than

tree.name: ResponsiveLayout
tree.doc:
A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. `share` divides the width (what is left of it
after the gaps) among the children it NAMES — the names are the view's own
child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is
a loud error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **`0` hides that child while
the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a
number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view
widens. A child a plan does NOT name is left alone: natural width, the flow
just places it. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry
its own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children
keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as
always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On
the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary
literals (`y = center` in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack
at all — *shares fill; naturals align.*

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages NAMED regions. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State` applied on a
width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding `place()` —
the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a
number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view
widens. A child a plan does NOT name is left alone: natural width, the flow
just places it. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry
its own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children
keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as
always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On
the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary
literals (`y = center` in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack
at all — *shares fill; naturals align.*

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages NAMED regions. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State` applied on a
width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding `place()` —
the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

attributes.name: plan
attributes.doc:
The storyboard: a list of `{ from, flow, share?, gap? }` entries. **`from` means "use
this plan when the view is at least this wide"** — the largest `from` that fits wins,
wherever it sits in the list, and `from: 0` is the fallback. `flow` is `"row"` or
`"stack"`. `share` divides the width among the children it **names by their own child
names**, checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error.
**A share of `0` hides that child while the plan is active**, so "the actions disappear
on small screens" is one number, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A
child a plan does not name keeps its natural width.

methods.name: place
methods.doc:

arranges accordingly. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much
room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A
plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business.

tree.name: Spacer
tree.doc:
When a row (or stack)
does not fill its container, the leftover space has to go SOMEWHERE — and
the laid children cannot take it themselves (their flow-axis slot is owned
by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two
groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each
side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns.
Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan
whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply
zero and invisible in effect.

The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so
a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the
`flexes` marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise —
it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

Spacer's size along the flow axis and expands it to take up the slack — which is

tree.name: Table
tree.doc:
The list collection, componentized (docs/system-design/component-briefs.md §2 —
D8 RULED): the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or
written) collection, carrying the RULED selection model
(docs/system-design/selection-model.md) so no app hand-rolls it again:

- **Selection is the Table's VALUE** — `selected` (the primary member) and
  `selection` (all of them, presented order), holding MEMBERS: the record for
  a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via
  `input` (Contract 1 form b); identity per the ruled ladder (a record's `id`
  by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule).
- **The three facts**: selection, the ANCHOR (where ranges extend from), and
  the keyboard position `active` — moved by arrows, extended by shift,
  walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection).
- **`selects` declares the mode**: `none | single | multi` (default single).
  (Build note: the ruled docs used one word for the mode AND the value; the
  value keeps the ruled name `selection`, so the mode rides `selects`.)
- Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children
  reaching their table as `parent`, replicated over data or written by hand.
  The row template stays free of any selection wiring.
- Windowing composes: put `virtualize` on the row template and selection,
  ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the DATA
  through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row
  can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (uniform
  row extents, the kernel's own v1 assumption).

    Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel },
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30,
            t: Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ] ] ]

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 200,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" },
                             { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" },
                             { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } },
    t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26,
            Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ]
            ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Combobox
tree.doc:
Filter-as-you-type over a collection (component-briefs.md §3 — D8 RULED): a
text field owning a QUERY plus a dismissable option list owning a CHOICE — the
canonical derived selection over data. Composition, not invention: TextInput
for the entry, the Menu machinery for the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss,
Escape closes — the whole dismissal discipline rides along), and the matches
are a DERIVED collection — a constraint over the items array, so the live
match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned.

    Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ]

- **Items are members** (the selection model's currency): records — shown by
  their `label` (or `id`) — or plain strings. `value` holds the CHOSEN member;
  `input(v)` is the delivery seam (Contract 1): the default writes `value`, a
  use-site override redirects and the slot stays untouched.
- **Typing filters live** (case-insensitive substring); opening WITHOUT typing
  shows the full list (the disclosure-button read). Picking echoes the label
  into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text.
- **Keyboard**: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved
  row — or the FIRST match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path);
  Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the
  focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own.
- The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and
  `virtualize` applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes).

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "",
    people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] },
    Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people },
        input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: ContextMenu
tree.doc:
The right-click / long-press menu (component-briefs.md §4 — D8 RULED): Menu's
machinery WHOLE — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport
clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (outside press closes AND is swallowed),
Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. No new overlay
machinery, by the brief's own constraint: if ContextMenu ever needs something
Menu lacks, Menu grows it and both ride.

Declared ONCE, opened by many. The SERVING view declares the gesture — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "",
    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }),
                                      ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }),
                                      ({ divider: true }),
                                      ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: DataGrid
tree.doc:
The Table contract plus a COLUMN MODEL (component-briefs.md §5 — D8 RULED):
headers, sortable, reorderable and resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a
windowed collection — the header drags are the forcing case the axis-scoped
`claim = x` was designed for.

    DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 70 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ]

- **Columns are written members** (`Column` — selection-model §1b: permanent,
  authored, identity = the child): `title` heads the column, `field` names
  what a cell shows, `width` is the authored width — a PLAIN value (the
  column model derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive
  width belongs in the grid's `widths` state, which IS a tracked dep:
  `widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }`). A column's id is its
  `field` (title as fallback).
- **Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state** (Contract 1 form b):
  `order` (column ids, presented order) and `widths` (id → width overrides).
  Reorder delivers through `arrangeInput(order)`, resize through
  `resizeInput(id, w)` — defaults write the slots; an app override owns them
  (persisted layouts). Widths are PLAIN VALUES — nothing measures cells.
- **Header interactions**: click sorts — a DELIVERY (`sortInput(on, dir)`
  writing `sortOn`/`sortDir` by default): sort NAMES a derivation, the truth
  stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the
  order its collection has). Horizontal drag REORDERS (live swap at the
  midpoint); the right-edge grip RESIZES. Both drags declare `claim = x` —
  on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x.
- **Rows**: the use site writes ONE bare `GridRow` template over its rows
  path — cells generate from the column model, each showing `record[field]`.
  Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — `virtualize` on the
  template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets
  the window's geometry (the kernel's leading anchor).
- Focus: land-as-one-stop, browse mode (arrows navigate rows). Entry-mode
  grids (`focusScope = capture`, the tax-form convention) are a later
  increment; nothing here forecloses it.
- AT: rows speak logical position (the Surface seam). The column dimension
  (`aria-colcount`/`colindex`) is DEFERRED to the same seam — noted, not
  wired, in v1.
- Narrow widths: v1 clips (`clip` on the cell); the deliberate degrade
  (priority, not squish) is a designed later increment per the brief.

Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are `Table`'s, documented there. What follows
is only the column model.

```declare
App [ width = 440, height = 220,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail",      "state": "open" },
                             { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" },
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 50 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]
        ]
    ]
```

Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize;
click a header to sort.

tree.name: Segmented
tree.doc:
A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options
are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are **data**, like
`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

```declare-fragment
Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page },
    choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }),
                 ({ id: "table",    label: "Table" }),
                 ({ id: "grid",     label: "DataGrid" }) ] },
    input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
    ]
```

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

It is also the mainstream shape. Most native toolkits take segments as titles in an array,
picks from a `ForEach`, Ant Design takes `options`; only Material and WinUI name
the item at all, and both compound it. A bare `Segment` class was the minority
pattern — and bare enough that two apps in this corpus had taken the name for a
paragraph of prose.

### Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a DESIGN decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view
tree, not the layout strategy whose job that is. Three reasons not to:

- **The systems that call this a segmented control agree.** The native ones
  divide evenly by default, as does the classic
  segmented `Picker`. The ones that size to content — Bootstrap, Ant — are really
  styling a row of buttons.
- **The segmented convention makes it a content rule**: keep segment labels short and
  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.
- **The sliding pill.** At equal widths it translates at constant width. At
  variable widths it would have to morph its width WHILE travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly: **a `Segmented` does not self-size to
its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

### The pill

The highlight springs a NORMALIZED LANE — a float index — not pixels. `x` is then
`lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes `segW` and the pill **snaps** to the right
place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. Calendar's tab
strip discovered this; it is the one thing the bespoke copies did better than the
library, and it is now here.

The look is the library's: the chosen segment wears a raised `surface` pill with
a hairline. The motion is calendar's. Neither app was wrong about the half it got
right (`chrome-divergences.md` D9).

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one",
    Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page },
        choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }),
                     ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }),
                     ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] },
        input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ]
    ]
```

`Menu`'s items use. A choice shows a label **or** an icon, never both. A choice may also
carry a `location`, which makes that segment a real link (see `SegmentedItem.location`).

attributes.name: value
attributes.doc:
The active choice. Bind it to your own state and override `input` to own the
destination, or leave it alone and read `value` back — a `Segmented` works
standalone. Compared against each item's `choice` by identity, so any value type
works.

attributes.doc:

attributes.name: angle
attributes.doc:

twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two
states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its
16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level `rotation` attribute turns the whole
box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.)

tree.name: Icon
tree.doc:
A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. Fonts are not UI objects:
their glyphs are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The house
already knew this in three places before it had a name for it (`Checkbox.mark`,
`Menu.check`, `Combobox.disc` are all drawn); this is that decision, stated once.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is ONE path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px, which is every site in this corpus, that is
invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a
mark — so **this set is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an
empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth =
weight` *outside* the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon
systems take a third road and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger
undertaking than this set needs.

`test/probe/iconbook.declare` shows the ramp — the same chevron and bulb at 16,
24, 32, 48 and 64 — if the tradeoff ever needs re-judging.

### What is NOT an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution
(`dom-backend.ts` `rasterize()`), while `scale` is a CSS transform applied
*after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them.
Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling
inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records AND reallocates the backing
canvas every frame, which is what dragged the dock's magnification from 60 to
~25fps (`adaptive-draw-cache.md`). A static size re-records once and costs
nothing after. Measured: 120 icons re-recording their *content* every frame runs
frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the prevailing text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets one — `IconHost` does it for
every icon built by name.

tree.name: IconHost
tree.doc:
A control names its icon (`iconLeft = TrashIcon`) rather than nesting one,
   because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and
   because an attribute is the one form where AUTHORED and BOUND are the same
   mechanism. `IconHost` is what turns that name into a live view, through the
   same `app.createView` seam the menu's `iconKind` already uses.

   It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only
   the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special
   case.

   LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction.
   A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not
   served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes
   on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this
   corpus names its icon statically.

that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

One choice of a `Segmented`, **materialized from that control's `choices` data — never
authored directly**, which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full

segments instead of popping.
